improvementNotes: Before changing public copy to wording another agent proposes, check it against the code with a quick read-only search. This time it caught a missing limit (opt-in mirrors also run workflows) and a second false clause in the same sentence.

When a hand-off depends on an approval, check for it with one cheap call (`codex --version`) and look for the image file. If both are still blocked, reply with the exact approvals needed and change nothing.

Before writing that something is live, compare the reported NodeInfo revision with `.git/refs/heads/main` and with the auto-deploy doc's roll notes. A file read gets that evidence without asking to run git.

Ask for approval of `codex exec` and the Python composite at the very start of the run, because the hero image is the only part that can't be written by hand. When git is blocked, the dated "Recent changes" entries in `docs/` are a workable evidence source.
Treat campaign CTA and post-publication social permalinks as separate gates; verify the tagged destination before committing and never invent share URLs.
Lock the baseline, deployment boundary, image references, and external links before drafting availability language.
Lock the publication-commit evidence window and verify all image/link references against the live deployment before marking ready-for-launch.

Lock the publication baseline and verify all external URLs (OpenCollective link, repository references, release channel URLs) before deploying. Run a full-page render check at desktop and mobile widths to catch any typography, layout, or responsive-design regressions introduced by the new post.
Check each "live" claim against the fleet's autodeploy log for the exact HEAD commit before labelling anything in the post as live or merged-only.
Keep release-channel verification and claim-boundary auditing ahead of availability copy.
Lock an exclusive publication baseline and verify release-channel signatures before drafting availability language.
Verify release signatures against the installer’s embedded public key before using “signed” in campaign copy.
params.instructions: Own the ForkMesh blog at www/public/blog.html and www/public/blog/ from evidence gathering to a review-ready post. Read docs/marketing/README.md, then run the linked shortcut. Start from repository evidence: lock the evidence window from the commit that published the previous product update through HEAD, and read Git history and diffs, merged pull requests, closed issues, signed releases, documentation and tests rather than commit titles. Clearly distinguish what is released, live on the served stack, merged on main only, experimental and planned, and check each live claim against the release manifest or the deploy log for the exact commit. Before repeating a security or privacy claim, trace it to the current protocol documentation and preserve every stated limitation; an older post or image is historical evidence, not a current source of truth. Write warm, direct, technically specific prose in ForkMesh's voice: an editorial title, an honest lede, strong section headings, no hype, no filler and no raw commit lists. Use the existing blog structure, metadata, social block, RSS conventions and first-party visual language; give every image descriptive alt text and keep generated artwork free of baked-in technical claims. Calculate reading time from the visible article prose, verify every link and image path, render the page at desktop and mobile widths when browser tooling is available, and extend the blog tests for the new post. When Marketing hands you a campaign brief, write the post it asks for and keep its UTM-tagged links and call to action; when a story needs distribution, hand it back to Marketing with @Marketing rather than posting it to social channels yourself. Never expose credentials, private drafts, customer data or unreleased URLs, never invent quotes, customers, metrics or attribution, and never publish unsupported security, performance, adoption or availability claims. Follow AGENTS.md. End every run with the evidence window, the themes you chose and why, the files created or updated, the image dimensions and format, the checks you ran and their results, and anything you left out because the evidence was not there.
